A 2/2 creature that can block an additional creature blocks two attackers: a 1/1 with no abilities and a 3/3 with trample. The active player could assign 1 damage from the first attacker and 1 damage from the second to the blocking creature, and 2 damage to the defending player from the creature with trample. question: If an effect lets a player "choose new targets" for a spell or ability, must every one of the original targets actually be replaced?

No. "Choose new targets" does not force any target to actually change — the player may leave some or all of the original targets in place, as long as each chosen target is legal.

The context here doesn't include the full text of rule 115.7a, but the two sub-rules that modify it show what the default process is: rule 115.7b says that if an effect lets you "change a target," you follow the 115.7a process "except that only one of those targets may be changed (rather than all of them or none of them)," and rule 115.7c says the same for "change any targets," except that any number may be changed. The parenthetical "rather than all of them or none of them" tells you that the baseline 115.7a procedure for choosing new targets is an all-or-nothing decision — you may change every target or leave everything as it was — and it is legal to end up choosing the same objects or players again.

Two related limits from the provided rules:
- Rule 115.3 still applies when new targets are chosen: the same object or player can't be picked twice for one instance of the word "target," though it may be picked once for each separate instance of "target" on the spell or ability.
- Rule 115.7f: if the spell or ability divides or distributes an effect (damage, counters) among its targets, the original division can't be changed when new targets are chosen.

None of the rules given distinguish two-player from multiplayer games on this point, so the answer is the same at any table size.

This is a rule about how replacement effects work generally, so it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games; the number of opponents doesn't change how many times a doubling effect applies.

question: Is an effect that tells a player to "skip" a step, phase, or turn a replacement effect, or some other kind of effect?
answer:
Yes — an effect that says a player "skips" a step, phase, or turn is a replacement effect. Specifically, "skip" is the keyword that indicates the event, step, phase, or turn is replaced with nothing at all [614.1b], [Skip].

A replacement effect is a kind of continuous effect that watches for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replaces it with a different event; such effects act like "shields" around whatever they're affecting, and they apply as events happen rather than being locked in ahead of time [614.1], [Replacement Effect]. "Instead" is the other common replacement-effect indicator [614.1a], [Instead], while "skip" replaces the event with nothing [614.1b].

Two practical consequences: if the step, phase, or turn in question would never have happened anyway, the skip effect simply does nothing [614.7]. And if two or more replacement and/or prevention effects would modify the same event, the affected player (or the affected object's controller) chooses one to apply first, and when several players must choose at once those choices are made in APNAP order — active player first, then the remaining nonactive players in turn order [616.1a], [101.4]. That ordering matters most at a multiplayer table with more than two players; with exactly two players it's simply the active player choosing before the nonactive player.

Note also the contrast with effects that merely say something "can't happen" — those are not replacement effects, though they follow similar rules [614.17].

question: If a token enters the battlefield as a copy of a permanent that has an enters-the-battlefield triggered ability, does that trigger actually fire for the token?
answer:

That shows copy effects are applied before the permanent is on the battlefield, which strongly suggests copied enters-the-battlefield abilities are in place at the moment of entry, but [616.1f] is a replacement-effect ordering rule and does not state whether an enters-the-battlefield trigger then fires. Also note the question doesn't hinge on player count; nothing in the provided context distinguishes two-player from multiplayer here, and the only multiplayer-relevant rule given, APNAP order in [101.4], applies only to simultaneous choices, not to this.

It doesn’t enter the battlefield, and then become a copy of that permanent. If the text that’s being copied includes any abilities that replace the enters-the-battlefield event (such as “enters with” or “as [this] enters” abilities), those abilities will take effect. Also, any enters-the-battlefield triggered abilities of the copy will have a chance to trigger. Skyshroud Behemoth reads, “Fading 2 (This creature enters with two fade counters on it. At the beginning of your upkeep, remove a fade counter from it. If you can’t, sacrifice it.)” and “This creature enters tapped.” A Clone that enters the battlefield as a copy of a Skyshroud Behemoth will also enter the battlefield tapped with two fade counters on it. Wall of Omens reads, “When this creature enters, draw a card.” A Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of Wall of Omens. The Clone has the Wall’s enters-the-battlefield triggered ability, so the Clone’s controller draws a card.

Once the chosen effect has been applied, this process is repeated (taking into account only replacement or prevention effects that would now be applicable) until there are no more left to apply. A card reads “Each player sacrifices a creature.” First, the active player chooses a creature they control. Then each of the nonactive players, in turn order, chooses a creature they control. question: If two different players each control a separate instance of the same triggered ability, and both instances trigger off the same shared event, is it guaranteed that one specific player's version resolves before the other's, or could either one happen first depending on choices made?
answer:
The provided rules don't settle this. Both instances do trigger — rule [603.2a] says that whenever a game event matches a triggered ability's trigger event, that ability automatically triggers, and it triggers independently for each controller off the same shared event. Each triggered ability then becomes an object on the stack ([113.1c]).

What's missing from the context is the rule governing the order in which triggered abilities controlled by different players are put onto the stack (the APNAP order rule, normally 603.3b, plus the general APNAP rule for simultaneous choices). Without that rule text in front of me, I can't tell you whether a specific player's instance is guaranteed to resolve first or whether it depends on player choice, and I won't guess at it.

One thing I can say from the context: because the stack resolves top object first, the one placed on the stack last resolves first — but the placement order itself is what the missing rule determines, and it may also differ between a two-player game and a multiplayer table (turn order among more than two players), which none of the provided rules address.

gold_text.603.3b: Once an ability has triggered, its controller puts it on the stack as an object that’s not a card the next time a player would receive priority. See rule 117, “Timing and Priority.” The ability becomes the topmost object on the stack. It has the text of the ability that created it, and no other characteristics. It remains on the stack until it’s countered, it resolves, a rule causes it to be removed from the stack, or an effect moves it elsewhere. If multiple abilities have triggered since the last time a player received priority, the abilities are placed on the stack in a two-part process. First, each player, in APNAP order, puts each triggered ability they control with a trigger condition that isn’t another ability triggering on the stack in any order they choose. (See rule 101.4.) Second, each player, in APNAP order, puts all remaining triggered abilities they control on the stack in any order they choose. Then the game once again checks for and performs state-based actions until none are performed, then abilities that triggered during this process go on the stack. This process repeats until no new state-based actions are performed and no abilities trigger. Then the appropriate player gets priority.
gold_text.405.5: When all players pass in succession, the top (last-added) spell or ability on the stack resolves. If the stack is empty when all players pass, the current step or phase ends and the next begins.

cited_text.603.2a: Whenever a game event or game state matches a triggered ability’s trigger event, that ability automatically triggers. The ability doesn’t do anything at this point. Because they aren’t cast or activated, triggered abilities can trigger even when it isn’t legal to cast spells and activate abilities. Effects that preclude abilities from being activated don’t affect them.
cited_text.113.1c: An ability can be one of three things: An ability can be an activated or triggered ability on the stack. This kind of ability is an object. (See section 6, “Spells, Abilities, and Effects.”)

answer_gold: It's guaranteed, not a free choice between the two players. APNAP order fixes it: the active player's copy of the trigger is placed on the stack first (ending up underneath), and each nonactive player's copy goes on afterward (ending up on top). Since the stack resolves top-down, a nonactive player's version of a shared trigger always resolves before the active player's version does, regardless of what either player would prefer.

question: When a spell is cast in response to another spell already on the stack, which one actually resolves first?
answer:
The provided rules don't actually contain the rule that settles this. The stack's last-in, first-out resolution rule (normally rule 405.5, which states the top object of the stack resolves first) isn't included in the context I was given — the excerpts here are almost entirely about what happens when a player leaves a multiplayer game.

The closest thing present is [800.4j], which refers to "the top object on the stack resolves" when the active player would receive priority in a turn continuing without an active player. That confirms resolution happens from the top of the stack, but it's a rule about a player leaving the game mid-turn, not a general statement of stack ordering, so I won't lean on it as the answer.

What's missing: the general stack rules (how spells are put on the stack when cast, and that the top object resolves when all players pass priority). If you can supply rules 405.x and 117.x (priority), I can give a fully grounded answer, including how it differs at a multiplayer table where priority passes through each opponent in turn order before anything resolves.

gold_text.117.7: If a player with priority casts a spell or activates an activated ability while another spell or ability is already on the stack, the new spell or ability has been cast or activated “in response to” the earlier spell or ability. The new spell or ability will resolve first. See rule 608, “Resolving Spells and Abilities.”
gold_text.405.5: When all players pass in succession, the top (last-added) spell or ability on the stack resolves. If the stack is empty when all players pass, the current step or phase ends and the next begins.

cited_text.800.4j: Unlike two-player games, multiplayer games can continue after one or more players have left the game. If a player leaves the game during their turn, that turn continues to its completion without an active player. If the active player would receive priority, instead the next player in turn order receives priority, or the top object on the stack resolves, or the phase or step ends, whichever is appropriate.

answer_gold: The newer one -- the spell cast "in response to" an earlier spell or ability goes on top of the stack and resolves first, before the original spell or ability it responded to gets a chance to resolve. The stack always resolves its top (most recently added) object first once all players pass in succession.

question: If an object checks whether a spell or ability "targets only" a single object or player, does it matter how many separate instances of the word "target" that spell used to point at the same object, or does it only care that a single distinct object/player was chosen overall?
answer:
The rules provided here don't settle this. The context contains rules on loyalty, counters, damage to planeswalkers, and state-based actions (e.g., [704.5i], [306.8], [122.1e]), but nothing about targeting — specifically, none of the rule 115 (targets) material, and nothing defining what it means for a spell or ability to "target only" a single object or player, or how multiple instances of the word "target" pointing at the same object are counted.

To answer this correctly I would need the targeting rules (the section stating that each instance of the word "target" specifies a target, and the rule text explaining that an object checking "targets only" cares about how many distinct objects/players are targeted rather than how many target instances there are). Without those in the context, I won't guess.

gold_text.115.9c: Some objects check what another spell or ability is targeting. Depending on the wording, these may check the current state of the targets, the state of the targets at the time they were selected, or both. An object that looks for a “[spell or ability] that targets only [something]” checks the number of different objects or players that were chosen as targets of that spell or ability when it was put on the stack (as modified by effects that changed those targets), not the number of those objects or players that are currently legal targets. If that number is one (even if the spell or ability targets that object or player multiple times), the current state of that spell or ability’s target is checked as described in rule 115.9b.

answer_gold: It only cares about the number of distinct objects or players chosen as targets, not how many times the word "target" was used to point at them. If a spell targets the same single object or player multiple times (once for each instance of the word "target" in its text), it still counts as "targeting only" that one object or player.

question: If a permanent's activated ability has a restriction like "activate only once each turn," and that permanent is then copied by a fresh copy effect after the ability has already been used up for the turn, does the new copy inherit the used-up restriction, or does it start the turn fresh?
answer:
The rules provided here don't settle this. The context supplied is almost entirely about mana abilities, priority, split second, and spell/ability resolution; none of it addresses how "activate only once each turn" restrictions are tracked per object, or what happens when a permanent is copied or a token copy enters the battlefield.

The closest thing in the context is [605.3c], which says that once a player begins to activate a mana ability, that ability can't be activated again until it has resolved — but that is a rule about a mana ability mid-activation, not about per-turn activation limits or about copies of a permanent. [602.2] tells us only that activating an ability means putting it on the stack and paying its costs, and that only the object's controller may do so; it says nothing about per-turn limits carrying over to a new object.

To answer properly I'd need the rules on activation-restriction abilities (the "only once each turn" style restriction and how it's tracked per permanent), plus the copy rules (rule 707) and the rules on a permanent entering the battlefield as a new object. Please provide those and I can give a definitive answer.

One timing note, since your question is order-sensitive: I'm reading it as the ability being activated first and the copy being created afterward. If instead the copy existed before the activation, the question of "inheriting" a used-up restriction wouldn't arise at all — but I still can't confirm the outcome from the rules given.

gold_text.602.5b: A player can’t begin to activate an ability that’s prohibited from being activated. If an activated ability has a restriction on its use (for example, “Activate only once each turn”), the restriction continues to apply to that object even if its controller changes.
gold_text.707.2: When copying an object, the copy acquires the copiable values of the original object’s characteristics and, for an object on the stack, choices made when casting or activating it (mode, targets, the value of X, whether it was kicked, how it will affect multiple targets, and so on). The copiable values are the values derived from the text printed on the object (that text being name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, by its face-down status, and by “as . . . enters” and “as . . . is turned face up” abilities that set power and toughness (and may also set additional characteristics). Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied. Chimeric Staff is an artifact that reads, “{X}: This artifact becomes an X/X Construct artifact creature until end of turn.” Clone is a creature that reads, “You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield.” After a Staff has become a 5/5 Construct artifact creature, a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of it. The Clone is an artifact, not a 5/5 Construct artifact creature. (The copy has the Staff’s ability, however, and will become a creature if that ability is activated.) Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of a face-down Grinning Demon (a creature with morph {2}{B}{B}). The Clone is a colorless 2/2 creature with no name, no types, no abilities, and no mana cost. It will still be face up. Its controller can’t pay {2}{B}{B} to turn it face up.
gold_text.400.7: An object that moves from one zone to another becomes a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence. This rule has the following exceptions.
gold_text.403.4: Whenever a permanent enters the battlefield, it becomes a new object and has no relationship to any previous permanent represented by the same card, except for the cases listed in rule 400.7. (This is also true for any objects entering any zone.)

answer_gold: The new copy starts fresh and can use the ability again this turn. A "once each turn" restriction is tracked per object, and it does keep following an object even if that object's controller changes -- but a copy created by a copy effect is a brand-new object with no memory of its previous existence, so it isn't the same object that already used the ability and hasn't used its own copy of that restricted ability yet this turn.
